questions.question: What happens if you declare a component inside another component's body?
options: Nothing, it is a normal pattern
React sees a new component type each render and remounts the subtree, losing its state
React throws a compile error
The inner component becomes a singleton
questions.explanation: A nested declaration creates a brand new function on every render. React treats it as a different component type, unmounts the old tree and mounts a new one, so state and focus are lost.

questions.question: Can a component change the props it receives?
options: Yes, props are mutable objects
No, props are read only and must not be modified by the receiving component
Only if the prop is an object
Only inside an event handler
questions.explanation: Props are read only. A component that mutates its props stops being predictable, which breaks React's rendering model. Derive a new value or ask the parent to change its state.

questions.question: How should a child component change a value that lives in its parent?
options: Assign to the prop directly
Call a function the parent passed down as a prop
Import the parent and call setState on it
Use a global variable
questions.explanation: Data flows down through props and events flow up through callbacks. The parent owns the state and passes a function the child can call.

questions.question: What is the children prop?
options: A list of every nested component in the tree
Whatever was placed between the component's opening and closing tags
An array of the component's state values
The component's own return value
questions.explanation: Anything written between the tags is handed to the component as `props.children`, which is what makes container components possible.

questions.question: What does the rest pattern do here?
options: It ignores every prop except variant
It collects all remaining props so they can be forwarded to the button element
It creates a copy of the children
It resets the props to their defaults
questions.explanation: `...rest` gathers every prop that was not destructured by name, so a wrapper can forward things like onClick and aria-label to the underlying element.

questions.question: When does a default value in the destructuring pattern apply?
options: Only when the prop is null
When the prop is missing or explicitly undefined
On every render regardless of the value
Only for string props
questions.explanation: Destructuring defaults fill in for `undefined`, which covers a prop that was not passed. A prop explicitly set to `null` keeps the null.

questions.question: Write a function that builds a class name
questions.explanation: Deriving values from inputs rather than mutating them is the same discipline props require.
